nameStory: The catbird grape gets its name from its association with catbirds, which are known to feast on the small, dark grapes this vine produces. The "cat" connection might also refer to the way this climbing vine can sneak around fences and boundaries like a prowling cat. Some folks call it Missouri grape since it's most common in the Missouri River valley region.
description: Catbird grape is a climbing woody vine that can scramble up trees, fences, and other supports using its curling tendrils. Like other wild grapes, it produces small clusters of dark purple grapes in late summer, though they're quite tart compared to store-bought varieties. This species is actually quite rare in New England, being much more at home in the southeastern and south-central United States. When you do find it, it's usually a vigorous climber that can reach impressive heights given the right support.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive hand-shaped leaves that give this species its scientific name 'palmata' (meaning palm-like). The leaves are deeply divided into 3-5 pointed lobes, feeling somewhat rough and fuzzy to the touch, especially on the underside.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A vigorous climbing vine that uses coiling tendrils to grab onto supports. The bark on older stems becomes shreddy and peels in strips, and the vine can grow quite thick with age.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small dark purple grapes hang in loose clusters in late summer. They're about the size of a pea and quite sour, with thick skins and prominent seeds inside.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers appear in small clusters in late spring. They're not showy but have a subtle sweet fragrance that attracts small insects.

idTips.label: Tendrils
idTips.description: Long, curling tendrils emerge opposite the leaves and coil around anything they can grab. They start green and flexible but become woody and brown with age.

habitat: In New England, catbird grape is extremely rare and likely represents introduced populations rather than native occurrences. When found, it typically grows in moist areas along streams, pond edges, or wet woodlands. It may also appear along fence lines or forest edges where it can find support to climb.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic hand-shaped form, and small clusters of tiny greenish flowers appear in late spring with a subtle sweet scent.
seasonality.summer: The vine is in full leaf, showing off its distinctive deeply-lobed foliage. Tendrils actively seek new supports to climb.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and small clusters of dark purple grapes ripen. The sour fruit may persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Bare woody stems show the characteristic shreddy bark, and old tendrils remain coiled around supports, helping with identification.

funFact: Despite being called catbird grape, the fruit is so sour that even most birds wait until after the first frost to eat them, when freezing converts some of the harsh acids into sugars, making them more palatable!
confusionNotes: With only 2 observations in New England, you're more likely to encounter other wild grapes like fox grape or riverbank grape. The key difference is catbird grape's deeply hand-shaped leaves - other wild grapes have leaves that are more heart-shaped or only shallowly lobed. Memory trick: "Catbird grape has cat-paw shaped leaves."
contextualKnowledge: Catbird grape is primarily a southern species, so any plants found in New England are likely escapees from cultivation or very unusual introductions. Most field guides focus on the more common native grapes like fox grape and riverbank grape, so finding a true catbird grape in New England would be quite a botanical discovery worth documenting.
compareHints: Among New England's wild grapes, catbird grape stands out for its deeply hand-shaped leaves with 3-5 distinct lobes, unlike fox grape's heart-shaped leaves or riverbank grape's more shallowly-lobed foliage. The leaf shape is really the key feature - while all wild grapes climb with tendrils and produce small sour grapes, only catbird grape has those distinctive "palm-shaped" leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's native grapes, fox grape stands out with its woolly white leaf undersides and slip-skin fruits.
Among New England's wild grapes, riverbank grape has the smallest, most tart fruit and the strongest preference for wet areas.
Summer grape stands out from other New England grapes primarily by its habitat preference for dry uplands rather than moist areas.

Wine grapes differ from native New England grapes primarily in their fruit - the clusters are much denser and tighter, and the individual grapes are noticeably sweeter with less of the tart, 'foxy' flavor characteristic of native species like fox grape.
Among New England's wild grapes, frost grape is distinguished by its reddish tendrils and the dramatic taste change after frost.
Among New England's wild grapes, graybark grape stands out for its uniquely dull, wrinkled leaves that feel soft and flabby rather than firm.
